I just Googled stuff. What I learned is you need to dilute the bleach, and a light mist is enough, don't drench the shirts. Obviously, starting with a less detailed design would give better results.

This guy put together a video showing his process, and he produces fantastic results. Using a cutter like he does is convenient, but his spraying process is the interesting part (you can start ~6 minutes in).

By far, the main gotcha to watch out for is getting the shirt too wet. The bleach will wick along the fibers, and get under your stencil. If the bleaching effect isn't strong enough, then let it evaporate before spraying more. You can speed that up a bit with an iron (although somebody on /r/bleachshirts recently mentioned corrosion on their iron from the bleach, so I guess that's a risk).
I use half bleach half water, you don't need very much of either

Welp, from psychology books, there's a few schools of thought, I'll attempt to outlay what each school of thought might say about it.

Psycho-dynamism

The person's unconscious mind desires something. Subconsciously, they believe the traits or abilities or social stigmas...etc. associated with the animal/thing would allow them to achieve their unconscious desire. Consciously, this manifests itself as a belief that the person is inhabited by/is one with the creature/thing. A sure sign that they have not achieved their goal will be that they still act like the creature/thing, and will only cease once they get what they desire, or find a better way to obtain it.

Behaviorism

The person acts like they are one with/ are inhabited by a creature/entity. The person is rewarded for this behavior. The person will continue to exhibit this behavior to continue to gain the reward until the reward stops. (unless we take addiction into play, and consider that if it only sometimes works, and the rate is random, they will continue doing it forever, even when they entirely stop receiving rewards for it)

Cognitive Psychology (used to be called Gestaltists)

They take much the same angle as the Behavioralists, but consider the thought process involved in how reward and punishment affect future reactions to stimuli:

Person wants attention.

Person acts like they are another creature/entity.

Someone becomes intrigued and converses with the person about it, enthusiastically.

Person now thinks: people will chat more with me like this, they find it interesting.

Later, Person comes across someone else, who thinks person is mentally ill.

Now the construct becomes: "some people like it, some people think I'm crazy"

For Person to continue to exhibit the behavior, Person will need to have met more people in support than against, or perhaps, someone who's opinion is held in high regard to Person is in support.

NeuroBiology

(which has apparently changed to something else since I studied Psychology)

It's all in the brain chemistry, specifically the balance of neurotransmitters, re-uptake inhibitors..etc. in various parts of the brain. They'd likely scan the brain activity via electroencephalography to see the activity compared to a normal brain in order to find any significant difference in activity levels. Or perhaps, with use of magnetic resonance imagery, they would look at various parts of the physical brain structure to find defects.

In a culture driven by independence, identity becomes the ultimate source of power. During human development, there is a stage when your sense of self, or personal identity, starts to solidify as one becomes an adult. When this process is stunted in adolescence, a person may not develop a strong sense of who they are and can have an identity crisis or develop borderline personality disorder.

A more common affliction is when the idea a person has of themselves does not agree with their reality, the result is angst. Pretty much everyone suffers from this in some way or another. We all deal, or not, with it in how we live our lives even if we are not aware of it.

Forming an identity around something that marks one as different or an outsider may be one way a person might make their internal identity match their external one to eliminate the pain of angst. Also, by becoming part of a group one trades intense loneliness and possibly ostracism for friends and community.

A person would also gain acceptance of possibly antisocial behavior... Not all communities are healthy.

Obligatory "not a psychologist", but I do study adolescent brain development, so close enough.

Adolescence is a crazy time. On almost every level, it's super unique. Your priorities change rapidly when you shift from being a kid into being an adult, different parts of your brain are developing very quickly at different rates, and all that combined with those pesky pubertal hormones. Moreover, there's this increased importance of social relationships during your teenage years. How important it is to have relationships with peers, and there's plenty of research to support this idea. Not having these close bonds can lead to neural abnormalities than can persist into adulthood.

Personally, I think the otherkin and tumblr crowd is just a bizarre reflection of this need for social relationships. It's something that you can identify with anonymously online and make new friends easily. I also think the idea that we don't seem to have any adults identifying this way or pushing for otherkin rights (unlike the transgender movement, for example) really suggests that this is a silly teenage fad that seems to exist in very small corners of the internet.

Moreover, with groups like r/TumblrInAction, I think a very large chunk of these online SJWs are just trolls making blogs. Not to say that the real hardcore SJWs don't exist, but I personally don't think they're as prominent as the internet would lead you to believe.

Article I found on Google Scholar: “We Are Spirits of Another Sort”: Ontological Rebellion and Religious Dimensions of the Otherkin Community Abstract

Otherkin are individuals who identify as “not entirely human.” Scholarship has framed this identity claim as religious because it is frequently supported by a framework of metaphysical beliefs. This article draws on survey data and interviews with Otherkin in order to provide a more thorough treatment of the phenomenon and to assess and qualify the movement's religious dimensions. It is argued that, in addition to having a substantively religious quality, the Otherkin community serves existential and social functions commonly associated with religion. In the final analysis, the Otherkin community is regarded as an alternative nomos—a socially constructed worldview—that sustains alternate ontologies.
